clue.text: Add variety with resounding performance in tower?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: vary what you do to avoid monotony
second meaning: bell-ringers in a church tower ringing the bells in changing sequences

explanation.surface: Someone livens things up with a booming show staged in a tower.
explanation.walkthrough: Change ringing is the English art of ringing church bells in constantly varied orders; the idiom for introducing variety comes from it.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to vary a routine, borrowed from bell-ringing where the order of the bells is constantly altered.

clue.text: Local restorers renovated fairground rides

indicators.note: something renovated has been taken apart and rebuilt, so the letters are put back together in a new order

explanation.surface: Local tradespeople have done up the rides at the funfair.
explanation.definitionFit: Roller coasters are a classic example of the thrill rides found at a fairground.

clue.text: Annual excuse for party — were any disturbed?

indicators.note: disturbed things are knocked out of their settled order, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether anyone was disturbed by the yearly celebrations.
explanation.definitionFit: The turn of the year comes round every twelve months and is the classic occasion for celebrating with friends.

clue.text: Prattled and made fun of the Queen coming in

indicators.note: one thing coming in to another ends up inside it

parts.note: to twit is to tease or taunt

explanation.surface: Someone chattered and mocked the monarch as she entered.
explanation.walkthrough: ER, for Elizabeth Regina, is the standard crossword Queen.
explanation.definitionFit: To twitter is to talk at length in a light, trivial, chattering way, just as birds do.

clue.text: Made effective use of page dropped by master journalist

indicators.note: something dropped is let go and left out, so a letter is removed

parts.note: a master of a craft is an expert

explanation.surface: A page went missing because of a senior reporter's actions.
explanation.walkthrough: The page's P is taken out of the master before the journalist is added.
explanation.definitionFit: To exert influence or strength is to bring it into action and use it to effect.

clue.text: Poisonous plant responsible for fowl pest?

parts.note: a hen is a domestic fowl
a bane is a curse or source of harm

explanation.surface: A toxic weed is blamed for a disease among poultry.
explanation.walkthrough: The plant's name was traditionally explained as being deadly to chickens, so the question mark flags a half-true etymology.
explanation.definitionFit: Henbane is a foul-smelling nightshade whose leaves and seeds are highly toxic.

clue.text: Green tea initially rejected by aborigine

indicators.note: what is rejected is thrown out, so that letter leaves the following word

parts.note: an aborigine is an original inhabitant

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letter of the word before it

explanation.surface: An Aboriginal Australian turns down a cup of green tea.
explanation.definitionFit: Green in the sense of inexperienced and gullible, as an innocent newcomer is.

clue.text: Changes wheels right away

indicators.note: sending something away removes it, so that letter is taken out

parts.note: wheels and revolves both mean turns round

explanation.surface: Someone swaps a car's wheels immediately.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Changes wheels' reads as a garage job, but wheels is a verb meaning turns.
explanation.definitionFit: To evolve is to develop gradually, which is a way of changing over time.

clue.text: Partial loss of sense that dressmaker's familiar with

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the tingling numbness of a limb that has gone to sleep
second meaning: the sharp tools a dressmaker handles every day

explanation.walkthrough: The medical first half hides the literal sewing kit of the second.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names the prickling sensation of reduced feeling in a limb, and literally the sharp sewing implements.

clue.text: Small pay increase needed for this type of housing

parts.note: low as in small in amount
British word for a raise in salary

explanation.surface: A modest wage rise is required to afford a certain kind of home.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a pay rise is what Americans call a raise.
explanation.definitionFit: Low-rise housing has only a few storeys, in contrast with tower blocks.

clue.text: Capital manner possessed by 50% of nobility

indicators.note: what is possessed is held inside, so one piece sits within the other
fifty per cent is a half, so only the front half of the next word is kept

parts.note: first four of its eight letters
an air is a manner or bearing

explanation.surface: Half of the aristocracy is said to have a grand, capital style.
explanation.definitionFit: Nairobi is the capital city of Kenya.

clue.text: Opt for standing, having changed sides

indicators.note: the two sides are left and right, so one is swapped for the other in the word

explanation.surface: Someone chooses to stand for election after switching parties.
explanation.walkthrough: The R of right in the word for upright becomes the L of left.
explanation.definitionFit: To elect is to choose, as voters select a candidate.

clue.text: Cockney criminals going to pot?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: rhyming slang, tea leaf for thief
second meaning: what goes into a teapot

explanation.walkthrough: Cockney rhyming slang is a London habit of replacing a word with a phrase that rhymes with it. 'Going to pot' sounds like decline, but is literal here.
explanation.definitionFit: Thieves in London rhyming slang, and also the dried leaves put into a pot to brew tea.

clue.text: Charge made by small bank on farm vehicle

explanation.surface: A fee is levied by a minor bank on a tractor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' in an across clue means the second piece follows the first. Charge and bank both look financial.
explanation.definitionFit: A cartridge holds the explosive charge and bullet for a gun.

clue.text: Girl from South Africa featured in tabloid …

indicators.note: something featured in a paper appears within it, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: The Sun, a British tabloid newspaper

explanation.surface: A South African girl appears in a popular newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sun is Britain's best-known tabloid paper.
explanation.definitionFit: Susan is a common female first name, so it fits a generic girl.

clue.text: Bent cop is for pocketing one narcotic

indicators.note: pocketing something puts it inside, so one piece goes within the other
bent means twisted out of shape, and also corrupt, so the letters are distorted

explanation.surface: A corrupt policeman is keen on pocketing a drug.
explanation.definitionFit: A soporific induces sleep, as narcotic drugs do.

clue.text: … posed in disguise, needing no introduction

indicators.note: with no introduction, the opening letter is not needed and is dropped

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue, the girl modelled in costume and needed no introduction.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links the surface to the previous clue only.
explanation.definitionFit: To pose a question is to ask it, so posed and asked are synonyms.

clue.text: Extremely keen Liberal leader dismissed as deceitful

indicators.note: dismissing the leader sends away whoever is in front, so the opening letter goes
the extremes of a word are its two ends, so only those letters are kept

explanation.surface: A very eager party leader is sacked for dishonesty.
explanation.walkthrough: Liberal looks like the political party but means generous.
explanation.definitionFit: A knave is a dishonest rogue, so knavish behaviour is dishonest and deceitful.

clue.text: Car wrecked in prison break could become this

definitions.text: Car wrecked in prison break could become this

indicators.note: to break something is to smash it apart, so the letters are scattered and reformed

explanation.surface: A getaway car smashed during a jailbreak would end up as metal junk.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the wordplay and the definition: a wrecked car is literally destined for the scrapyard.
explanation.definitionFit: A wrecked car is sold for its metal, ending up as discarded iron for recycling.

clue.text: Woman with two articles to put in case

parts.note: the indefinite article A and the definite article THE

explanation.surface: A woman takes two items to pack in a suitcase.
explanation.definitionFit: To sheathe a blade is to put it into its protective cover or scabbard.

clue.text: Flag with scarlet border pulled out

indicators.note: a border runs around the edge, so one piece surrounds the other

parts.note: to flag is to tire or weaken

explanation.surface: A banner edged in red was taken down.
explanation.walkthrough: Flag looks like a banner but is the verb meaning to grow weary.
explanation.definitionFit: To retire is to withdraw, as troops pulled out of a battle or a player pulled out of a race.

clue.text: Letter I posted includes reply

indicators.note: the phrase before it holds the letters inside it, spanning the words

parts.note: spans the end of the first word and most of the third

explanation.surface: A letter that someone mailed contains an answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A riposte is a quick, sharp retort, a kind of reply.

clue.text: Temporary coach directed first person further back

indicators.note: moving something further back shifts it to a later spot, so it is taken out and reinserted down the line

explanation.surface: A short-term coach steered the leading figure toward the rear.
explanation.walkthrough: The two words joined have an I in the fourth spot; it moves back two places, past the S.
explanation.definitionFit: Transient means passing quickly or lasting only a short time, so it is a synonym of temporary.

clue.text: Direct course of animal on farm

definitions.meaning: first meaning: guide the path of
second meaning: a young castrated bull

explanation.walkthrough: The verb and the noun share a spelling but nothing else.
explanation.definitionFit: To steer is to guide a vehicle's direction, and a steer is a bullock raised for beef.

clue.text: Indian bread and water passed after game

explanation.surface: Someone has naan and a drink after a match.
explanation.walkthrough: Bread is slang for money, not food; RU is rugby union.
explanation.definitionFit: The rupee is the currency of India, and bread is informal slang for money.

clue.text: Intend to wear torn old clothes

indicators.note: a garment that is worn goes around the wearer, so one piece envelops the other

parts.note: rent is an old past participle of rend, to tear

explanation.surface: Someone plans to put on ragged, worn-out garments.
explanation.definitionFit: Raiment is an archaic word for clothing, hence old in the sense of an old-fashioned term.

clue.text: No match official's expected to lose heart!

indicators.note: the heart is the very centre of a word, so losing it removes the middle letter

parts.note: what is usual is what is expected

explanation.surface: A referee is bound to feel discouraged by the poor game.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is read as 'is', a link; the heart of the five-letter word is its third letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying no is a refusal, a declining of a request.

clue.text: Spooner's poultry kept by Roald, a classic author

indicators.note: Spooner was famous for swapping the opening sounds of neighbouring words

parts.note: Roald Dahl's chickens, with their initial sounds swapped

explanation.surface: A children's author keeps hens that apparently belong to a famous novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: Roald Dahl wrote Charlie and the Chocolate Factory; swap the D and CH of 'Dahl's chickens'.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Dickens, author of Oliver Twist and Great Expectations, is a towering classic Victorian novelist.
